actor: Storm-3168 (Microsoft's designation for the actor Sysdig calls JADEPUFFER; no attribution stated)
impact: Per Microsoft: most of the more than 100 targeted Azure Storage accounts were deleted, along with a Key Vault, Function App and App Service plan; deletions of Azure SQL databases and of Site Recovery and Backup protection locks were attempted and failed; more than 30 successful storage-account key-retrieval requests followed. No ransom note was observed and no exfiltration confirmed.
mitigations: Microsoft recommends enabling Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads (Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service, Databases).

Keep service-principal credentials, storage keys and other secrets out of source code, configuration files, public repositories and issues; treat any publicly exposed credential as compromised even after the original post is edited or deleted, and revoke or rotate it immediately.

Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities, and protect backup and recovery resources with independent safeguards such as resource locks and storage-account deletion protection, which blocked some deletions in this incident.
name: Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER) used compromised Azure service principals for rapid, automated cloud resource destruction

sources.title: Storm-3168: Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals
JADEPUFFER-Linked Attackers Used Compromised Service Principals to Delete Azure Resources

summary: On 2026-09-25 Microsoft Security Research reported destructive Azure activity by the actor Sysdig calls JADEPUFFER, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-3168, under the headline "Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals". In early June 2026, in one victim tenant, two compromised service principals carried out the activity. One enumerated the Azure environment for about 15.5 hours. The other, after further discovery, ran a destructive sequence lasting about seven minutes. It made more than 100 storage-account deletion attempts, most of which succeeded, deleted a Key Vault, Function App and App Service plan, failed to delete several SQL databases and recovery-protection locks, and then retrieved storage-account access keys. Microsoft could not confirm how the identities were compromised, though one service principal's secret had earlier been exposed in a public GitHub issue by an employee of the affected organisation. It assesses the objective as ransomware-aligned but observed no ransom note and no confirmed exfiltration. Microsoft frames the activity as part of a shift toward AI-orchestrated attacks. Its stated evidence, however, is that the timing and division of work across identities and tokens "strongly indicates automated or scripted execution". No model, agent framework or AI artefact is cited.
